references.text: The psalmist describes how the kings of the earth and their rulers conspire against the Lord and his Anointed – a prophetic parallel to the conspiracy of the chief priests and scribes against Jesus ([ref:Sal 2:2|Psalms 2:2]).
Matthew's parallel account that the chief priests and elders gathered and plotted to arrest Jesus by deceit and kill him ([ref:Matt 26:3-5|Matthew 26:3-5]).
Mark's parallel account that the chief priests and scribes sought a way to arrest Jesus by deceit and put him to death, but feared the crowd ([ref:Mark 14:1-2|Mark 14:1-2]).

In John's Gospel, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered the council and decided that Jesus must die, so that the whole nation would not believe in him – a parallel to the plot in Luke 22:2 ([ref:Joh 11:47-53|John 11:47-53]).

Earlier, the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people sought to put Jesus to death, but they could not find how, because all the people clung to him and listened to him – the same fear of the crowd mentioned here ([ref:Luk 19:47-48|Luke 19:47-48]).
The scribes and chief priests wanted to arrest Jesus immediately, but they feared the crowd – a recurring theme that also characterizes Luke 22:2 ([ref:Luk 20:19|Luke 20:19]).

Peter explains in his Pentecost sermon that Jesus was handed over according to God's set purpose and foreknowledge, and that lawless men crucified and killed him – the fulfillment of what the chief priests planned ([ref:Apg 2:23|Acts 2:23]).
The prophecy about the suffering servant of the Lord who was despised and rejected by people – the background for the leaders' desire to remove Jesus ([ref:Jes 53:3|Isaiah 53:3]).
